elements.content: Course Overview

• Why HTML is the foundation of web development

• Learning goals for this session

• Brief agenda of topics covered

actions.text: Good morning, everyone! I'm Dr. Maya Patel, and today we're kicking off our journey into web development by exploring why HTML is the foundation of everything you see online.
First, notice the bullet points on the screen. We'll cover three main ideas: why HTML matters, the learning goals for this session, and a quick look at the agenda.
HTML gives structure to web pages—think of it as the skeleton that holds everything together. Without it, browsers wouldn't know where headings, paragraphs, or images belong.
By the end of today, you'll be able to write basic HTML tags, understand how they create page structure, and see how this knowledge prepares you for CSS and JavaScript later.
So, let's dive in and start building the building blocks of the web together.

elements.content: Basic HTML Document Structure

• <!DOCTYPE html> declaration

• Root <html> element

• <head> with <title>

• <body> for visible content

actions.text: Alright everyone, let’s dive into the basic structure of an HTML document. This is the foundation for every web page you’ll build.
First, the <!DOCTYPE html> declaration tells the browser that this is an HTML5 document. Next, the <html> element wraps everything on the page.
Inside <html>, we have the <head> section, where we place the <title> tag. The title appears on the browser tab and helps identify the page.
Finally, the <body> section holds everything you want visitors to see—text, images, links, and more.
So, to recap: declaration, root <html>, <head> with <title>, and <body> with visible content. That’s all you need for a minimal HTML page.

elements.content: Headings and Paragraphs

• Heading tags <h1>–<h6>: define hierarchy

• Paragraph tag <p>: body text

• Best practice: one <h1> per page

actions.text: Alright, everyone, let’s dive into headings and paragraphs, the building blocks of any web page.

First, we have the heading tags <h1> through <h6>. These create a hierarchy—<h1> is the most important title, and the numbers get smaller as the sections become less prominent. Using them correctly helps both readers and search engines understand the structure of your content.
A best practice to remember is to use only one <h1> per page, typically for the main title, and then cascade down with <h2>, <h3>, and so on.

Next, the paragraph tag

wraps regular body text. It tells the browser that the enclosed words form a paragraph, adding appropriate spacing and line breaks.
When you combine these tags, you get a clean, semantic structure that’s easy to read, easy to style, and easy for assistive technologies to navigate. Any questions before we move on?

elements.content: Links and Images

• <a href="..."> for navigation

• <img src="..." alt="..."> with alt text

• Relative vs. absolute URLs

<a href="https://example.com">Link</a>

<img src="image.png" alt="Description">

actions.text: Alright, let's dive into Links and Images. These are the building blocks that let us connect pages and add visual content to our web pages.

First, the anchor tag  creates a hyperlink that users can click to navigate to another page or resource. Next to it, the image tag  embeds a picture, and the alt attribute provides a text description for accessibility.
Here's a concrete example: Link to Example will take you to that site, while displays an image with a helpful description for screen readers.

Finally, remember the difference between relative URLs, which point to files within the same website folder structure, and absolute URLs, which include the full web address. Using the right type keeps your links reliable.
Great job! You've just learned how to add hyperlinks and embed images, essential skills for creating interactive and visually rich web pages.

elements.content: Lists: Ordered and Unordered
Introduce list structures for grouping items.

• Ordered list <ol> with automatic numbering

• Unordered list <ul> with bullet points

• List items defined with <li>

actions.text: Welcome back, everyone. In this part of our HTML basics we’ll explore how to group items using ordered and unordered lists.
First, an ordered list uses the <ol> tag. The browser automatically numbers each <li> item for you, so you don’t have to type the numbers yourself.
Next, an unordered list uses the <ul> tag. Instead of numbers you get bullet points, which are great for items that don’t need a sequence.
Finally, every list—whether ordered or unordered—contains individual list items defined with the <li> tag. Each <li> represents one entry in your list.
To recap, we have three key pieces: the <ol> tag for numbered lists, the <ul> tag for bullet lists, and the <li> tag for each list item. Any questions before we move on?

elements.content: Creating Tables

• Table container <table>

• Rows <tr>, header cells <th>, data cells <td>

• Simple table example for tabular data

<table>
  <tr>
    <th>Header 1</th> <th>Header 2</th>
  </tr>
  <tr>
    <td>Data 1</td> <td>Data 2</td>
  </tr>
</table>

actions.text: Alright everyone, let's dive into creating tables in HTML. This is a fundamental skill for organizing data on a web page.
First, we need a table container using the <table> tag. Inside it, each row is defined with <tr>, header cells with <th>, and regular data cells with <td>.
Here’s a simple example: we open a <table>, add a <tr> for the header row with three <th> cells, then another <tr> with three <td> cells for the data. This creates a basic three‑column table.
Notice how each tag pairs up—opening and closing—just like we did with lists earlier. Try writing this markup in your editor; you’ll see the table appear instantly.
To recap, we use <table> as the container, <tr> for rows, <th> for headers, and <td> for data cells. That’s all you need to build a simple table.

elements.content: Forms Basics

• Form container: <form>

• Input types: text, email, submit

• Accessible labels: <label>

• Textarea and button elements

actions.text: Good morning, everyone! I’m Dr. Maya Patel. Today we’ll explore the basics of HTML forms—how we collect information from users on a web page.
First, every form starts with a <form> container. This tag tells the browser that the elements inside are part of a single data‑collection unit.
Inside the form we use different input types. The most common are <input type="text"> for plain text, <input type="email"> which validates email addresses, and <input type="submit"> to send the data.
For accessibility, each input should have a matching <label> element. The label’s for attribute links to the input’s id, allowing screen readers to announce the purpose of the field.
When we need larger text areas, we use the <textarea> tag, and for clickable actions other than submit we can add a <button> element.
To recap, a basic form consists of a <form> container, appropriate input types, accessible labels, and optional textarea or button elements. Any questions before we move on?

elements.content: Semantic HTML

• Structural tags: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <section>, <article>, <footer>

• Improves screen‑reader navigation

• Promotes clean, maintainable code

actions.text: Alright everyone, let's dive into Semantic HTML and see why the tags we choose matter so much.
First, we have structural tags like <header>, <nav>, <main>, <section>, <article>, and <footer>. These tags tell browsers and assistive tools the role each part of the page plays.
When we use these tags, screen‑readers can jump straight to the navigation or main content, making the site much easier for users with visual impairments.
Plus, search engines understand the page structure better, which can improve our SEO rankings.
Finally, writing with semantic tags keeps our code clean and maintainable, so future developers—or even ourselves—can quickly grasp the layout.
Any questions before we move on to the next topic?

elements.content: Best Practices & Code Formatting

• Use meaningful headings and alt text

• Indent code for readability

• Validate HTML with online tools

• Keep structure logical and consistent

actions.text: Now let's explore best practices for clean, accessible HTML code.
First, always use meaningful headings and descriptive alt text so everyone, including screen‑reader users, can understand the page structure.
Second, indent your code consistently; this makes it easier to see nested elements and spot errors.
Third, run your HTML through an online validator to catch missing tags or attribute mistakes before publishing.
Finally, keep your page structure logical and consistent—group related sections, use semantic tags, and avoid unnecessary nesting.
Any questions so far? Feel free to ask; clear code helps everyone collaborate more smoothly.

questions.question: You are building a simple blog page. Briefly describe which HTML5 semantic tags you would use for the header, main article content, sidebar with related links, and footer, and explain why each tag is appropriate.
questions.commentPrompt: Rubric: (1) Identify header tag (e.g., <header>) - 25% (2) Identify main article tag (e.g., <article> or <main>) - 25% (3) Identify sidebar tag (e.g., <aside>) - 25% (4) Identify footer tag (e.g., <footer>) and provide clear rationale for each - 25%
questions.analysis: A strong answer mentions <header> for the top branding/navigation, <main> or <article> for the primary blog post content, <aside> for related links or secondary information, and <footer> for copyright and site‑wide links, with brief justification for semantic meaning.

actions.text: Alright, everyone, this is our final quiz for today’s session. It’s a quick way to see how well you can apply the HTML tags and spotting common markup errors we just practiced.

For the first question, remember the semantic purpose of each tag. The <nav> element is specifically designed to contain a block of navigation links, making it the most appropriate choice for a menu of links.

The second question tests your eye for detail. Notice that the second <li> tag is not closed – that’s a clear error. The other options are fine: the <ul> can follow a paragraph, the <div> is properly closed, and "container" is a perfectly acceptable class name.

For the short‑answer scenario, think about the main sections of a blog page. Use <header> for the top branding and navigation, <main> (or <article> for the core post), <aside> for related links or a sidebar, and <footer> for the bottom information. Each tag tells browsers and assistive tools what role that part of the page plays.
Great work! Review your answers, and if anything feels unclear, we’ll discuss it together now.

blocks.question: You are building a simple blog page. Briefly describe which HTML5 semantic tags you would use for the header, main article content, sidebar with related links, and footer, and explain why each tag is appropriate.
blocks.explanation: A strong answer mentions <header> for the top branding/navigation, <main> or <article> for the primary blog post content, <aside> for related links or secondary information, and <footer> for copyright and site‑wide links, with brief justification for semantic meaning.

blocks.text: Alright, everyone, this is our final quiz for today’s session. It’s a quick way to see how well you can apply the HTML tags and spotting common markup errors we just practiced.

For the first question, remember the semantic purpose of each tag. The <nav> element is specifically designed to contain a block of navigation links, making it the most appropriate choice for a menu of links.

The second question tests your eye for detail. Notice that the second <li> tag is not closed – that’s a clear error. The other options are fine: the <ul> can follow a paragraph, the <div> is properly closed, and "container" is a perfectly acceptable class name.

For the short‑answer scenario, think about the main sections of a blog page. Use <header> for the top branding and navigation, <main> (or <article> for the core post), <aside> for related links or a sidebar, and <footer> for the bottom information. Each tag tells browsers and assistive tools what role that part of the page plays.
